accuracy.evidence: Feeling words and strategies match CASEL self-awareness and self-management competencies and the England relationships and health education guidance for primary (recognise and talk about feelings using varied vocabulary, simple self-care strategies). The distinction taught, disappointed as a hope that did not happen versus angry at something unfair, follows standard emotion-vocabulary resources; slow breathing with longer out-breaths as a calming strategy is supported by paced-breathing research.

misconceptions.evidence: Addresses common confusions for five to eight year olds: calling every unpleasant feeling angry or sad (four scenes needing frustrated, disappointed, anxious, overwhelmed), mixing up angry and disappointed when nobody is to blame (rain-stops-the-picnic prediction), thinking the answer to overwhelm is to rush everything at once, believing fast breaths or holding your breath calms you, and treating hitting or shouting as coping strategies.

lab_distinct.evidence: Five feelings-specific mechanics: naming the feeling for illustrated scenes, sorting situations into an Angry jar or a Disappointed jar, piling jobs into a school bag while a feelings meter rises and then settling it by doing one job at a time, pressing and holding to breathe a balloon up slowly for three breaths, and choosing safe cards for a calm-down toolbox. No other lesson has a meter, breathing hold or toolbox; distinctness overlap was about 8 percent.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child experiences the ideas instead of hearing them: the meter climbs as more jobs go in the bag and drops only as single jobs are done, the balloon grows only if each breath is held at least 1.5 seconds, and unsafe toolbox cards are refused with a reason. Naming comes first, so later strategies are linked to the word the child chose.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions: angry or disappointed when rain stops a picnic, whether doing everything at once or one job at a time settles a too-full bag, and whether fast or slow breaths calm you. The tempting option is the instinctive one, and each reveal names the child's pick before the lab shows what works.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions (friend ill for the party, waiting for the swing, lots of people talking, which breathing, what a strategy is, a puzzle piece that will not fit) each with a targeted message: 'Angry fits when something is unfair. Nobody did this on purpose: it is a hope that did not happen.', 'Fast breaths keep you wound up. Slow breaths settle your body.', 'That could hurt someone or make it worse. Pick the calm way.'

readability.evidence: Kid explanation measured about grade 1.4 and the adult text grade 7.4 after the long adult sentences were split; both meet the family targets. Feeling words are each defined in a few plain words on screen (overwhelmed: too much at once; strategy: a plan you can use).

no_filler.evidence: The content gate passed with no filler phrases. Each paragraph teaches one feeling word, one difference or one strategy, and the adult text lists the specific mistakes and a calm-time routine for practising feeling words at home.

mobile.evidence: Headless walkthrough completed all six steps and the challenge without errors. Android light and iPhone screenshots were checked; overlapping job cards, jobs reappearing after being done and toolbox text spilling past cards were found and fixed, and the job list was tightened so it no longer touches the status text. Young layout gives 56px buttons and the hold-to-breathe target is the whole balloon.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light and dark themes. Every drag and the breathing hold have labelled button alternatives, a polite live region reports progress such as jobs in the bag and breaths taken, the canvas has an aria-label, and reduced motion shortens the auto-advance and demo delays.
